opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think interns are really one of the lifebloods of a research lab, especially in an industrial setting.

The first reason is fresh perspective. When you've been working in a company for a while, you naturally start to think in terms of products, roadmaps, what's feasible with the current infrastructure. That's valuable, but it can also narrow your imagination. PhD students come in with ideas from their academic labs and from reading papers broadly, and they're often willing to try things that a full-time researcher might dismiss too quickly as "probably won't work." Some of the most interesting projects we've done started from an intern asking a naive-sounding question.

The second reason is energy and focus. An internship is usually about three months, sometimes a bit longer, and the student comes in really wanting to accomplish something concrete, often a paper or a strong prototype. That time pressure creates a lot of momentum. For the full-time researchers mentoring them, it also forces us to scope problems clearly and to stay hands-on with the latest techniques, because you can't mentor well if you're out of touch.

Third, it's a two-way bridge with academia. Interns go back to their universities and carry with them a sense of what problems matter at scale, what compute and data make possible. And we learn from them what's happening in different academic groups. Over time that builds a network, and many of our best full-time hires actually started as interns. You've already worked together, you know each other's style, so it's a very natural pipeline.

And finally, I think it keeps the culture honest. Having students around reminds everyone that research is about curiosity and learning, not just shipping. In a field moving as fast as generative AI and physical AI, that openness to new ideas is something you really can't afford to lose.

fable-5.1.text:
Interns bring fresh energy into the lab. When you've been working in an industrial setting for years, you develop certain habits of thinking, certain assumptions about what's possible and what's not. Students coming from universities haven't absorbed those assumptions yet. They ask naive questions, and sometimes a naive question is exactly the one nobody inside has dared to ask.

There's also a practical side. Research in generative AI moves extremely fast. Interns come from different academic groups, so they carry the latest ideas from their advisors and their labs. In a sense, every summer we get a snapshot of what the whole academic community is thinking about. That exposure is very valuable for a team that might otherwise get too focused on its own roadmap.

And for the interns themselves, an industrial lab offers something universities often can't: compute at scale, large datasets, and the chance to see how an idea goes from a paper to something people actually use. Many of our best full-time researchers started as interns. They already know the culture, they know the problems, and we already know how they think. So it's not only about vitality in the moment. It's how the lab renews itself over time.

astra-6.text:
I think interns bring fresh perspectives. When you work on a problem for a long time, you develop assumptions about what will work and what won’t. A student coming in may ask, “Why do you do it this way?” That question can push the team to reconsider an approach or try something new.

And the exchange goes both ways. Interns get to work with researchers and see the practical constraints of industrial research, while the team gets exposed to different ideas and ways of thinking. If you give interns meaningful problems and room to explore, they become research collaborators. That helps keep a lab curious and willing to take risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interns bring fresh perspectives and a willingness to question assumptions. In an industrial lab, it’s easy to become focused on established projects and immediate needs. Students come in asking, “Why do we do it this way?” Sometimes that question opens up a new research direction.

It’s also a two-way exchange. They get to work on problems with real constraints, and we learn from the ideas and approaches they bring. Giving them room to explore, while providing good mentorship, helps keep the lab curious and willing to experiment. That’s essential for research vitality.
